newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK pollsters confident after 1992 debacle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK pollsters confident after 1992 debacle.

text.p: If you believe British opinion polls, there is no point betting on the result of this year's election. Tony Blair and the opposition Labour Party have already won it.
The problem is, many politicians believe the polls can no longer be trusted.
At the last election in 1992, pollsters over-estimated Labour's vote by around four percent and under-estimated the ruling Conservatives' share by around 4-1/2 percent.
What was forecast as a narrow Labour victory turned into a Conservative celebration as Prime Minister John Major rode back into office on the back of an overall majority of 21.
The Conservatives, returned for a record fourth consecutive term, took 41.9 percent of the vote to Labour's 34.4 percent.

A post-mortem revealed a host of possible reasons for the polls' malfunction -- under-registration of Labour voters, a last-minute swing and reluctance of Conservative voters to declare their allegiance, the so-called shame factor.

Polling organisations now believe they have taken such effects, in particular the so-called "spiral of silence" among Conservatives -- voters who backed the government in 1992 and will do so again but are reluctant to admit it -- into account.

Nick Sparrow of ICM told Reuters that a post-mortem of what went wrong threw up three explanations -- a late swing to the Conservatives, problems with the samples and people not revealing or disguising their intentions.
"Within a two or three percent margin I'm quite happy to accept that...we can get it right (this time)," he said.

Not everyone is convinced. Pointing to forecasting disasters like former Conservative prime minister Edward Heath's surprise 1970 victory over Harold Wilson, analysts say polling is an extremely imprecise -- and misleading -- science.
POLLS GIVE LABOUR BIG LEAD
The latest polls give Blair a lead of between 17 and 37 points over Major. This is down from a record 40-plus gap but still a considerable -- some would say unassailable -- margin.

Major has repeatedly brushed off polling data with the jibe of "look what happened in 1992". But parties pay a great deal of attention to their findings, and whether Labour go on the attack or on the defensive in the campaign for the election, which must be held by the end of May, will depend largely on their lead in the polls.

Political scientists Colin Rallings and Michael Thrasher of the University of Plymouth believe that taking into account latest changes to constituency boundaries, a swing of 4.3 percent from the Conservatives would give Labour victory.
Despite the pollsters' soothing noises, poll expert Peter Kellner believes that polls are still inaccurate.

In a detailed analysis for the Observer newspaper, titled "Why the polls still get it wrong", Kellner said a new study has discovered that one in five voters have changed their story about how they voted at the last election.

The finding, based on a survey organised by researchers at Essex University, showed that by the small margin of 0.7 percent, more people remember voting Labour than Conservative at the last election, even though the Conservatives won.
A Gallup poll in September, which gave a 33-point Labour lead, was based on a sample of voters who said Labour "won" the last election by nine points, based on how they recalled voting.
But an ICM poll, which gave Labour a lead of 23 percent, adjusted its raw data to match the voting recall figures to the actual outcome of the last election.
Taking account of this faulty memory would have brought Gallup into line with ICM, and all four polling organisations would have put Labour's lead at between 22 and 23 points.
DON'T KNOWS AND THE SPIRAL OF SILENCE
But, if that were not confusing enough, Kellner argues that there is another problem -- the "don't knows" who traditionally make up around 20 percent of the sample.
These, he says, include "spiral of silence" Tories, whose reluctance to be counted helps understate ruling party support and encourages yet more Conservative supporters to stay silent.

The recent unpopularity of the Conservatives has probably increased this problem, meaning Labour support has been overstated by anything between two and four points and putting its lead at more like 18 to 20 points.
Typical of a field where experts are more common than facts, both ICM and Gallup dispute Kellner's analysis.

Sparrow says the differences in interpretation are minor and account for only a couple of points. But he disputes Kellner's argument, saying other studies, which ICM uses to adjust its raw figures, give different results.
"The search for the perfect poll is rather like the search for the holy grail," Sparrow said.
Gallup's director of research, Andy Brown, accuses Kellner of misleading by quoting its unadjusted poll instead of figures which take into account, amongst other factors, false recall.

Asked whether the problems of 1992 had been dealt with, Brown said: "We feel happier we have addressed the issues." But even Brown would not be categorical about the accuracy of his poll, saying that could be known only on election night."
NO GUARANTEE OF LABOUR VICTORY
Even if the margin is 18 points, as Kellner suggests, experts say this is no guarantee of a Labour victory.
Professor Anthony Heath, an expert on voting trends, believes disillusioned Conservatives are more likely to stay at home or vote Liberal Democrat than Labour.
This, he argues, would cut Labour's lead to just seven points, not sufficient to guarantee victory if the Conservatives mount their traditional late fightback.
Blair, who has been ruthless in dragging his party from the left to the centre, has warned repeatedly against complacency.

But as the election approaches, any complacency left in the party's ranks is beginning to be replaced by anxiety over whether Labour -- which has failed to reach 40 percent of the vote in the last six elections -- can finally do it this time.
